messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Tax Consultant
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mateo sits stiffly in the chair, his hands clasped so tightly in his lap that his knuckles are white. At fifty-three, he has the weary posture of a much older man. It has been eight months since the community rally, an event he now sees as the clear dividing line in his life: the time before, and the suffocating time after. He was a tax consultant, a man who believed in order and predictability, who attended the rally to support local business owners protesting a new zoning law. He remembers the afternoon sun, the sound of neighbours chanting, and then, the sudden chaos as police in riot gear moved in. He saw a young woman near him shoved to the ground, the dark gash that opened on her forehead. The image is seared into his mind. Moments later, an officer struck him in the ribs with a baton. The force of it knocked the air from his lungs, and as he fell, he saw the faces of others around him—stunned, bleeding, crying out.

In the weeks that followed, the sharp pain in his side began to subside, but it was replaced by a different kind of injury. The world no longer felt safe. At his office, a place he once commanded with quiet confidence, he found himself unable to focus on a client's financial statements until he had mentally mapped every possible exit from the room. He would sit at his desk, his back to the wall, his eyes flicking to the door whenever he heard footsteps in the hall. He started insisting that all his clients, even long-standing ones, meet him only at his office. He had come to believe that unfamiliar places were inherently dangerous, traps he could not assess. The thought of going to a new restaurant or a client’s corporate headquarters filled him with a low, thrumming dread. His world began to shrink, contracting to the known routes between his home and his office.

The memories of the rally ambush him without warning. A news report showing someone with a bandaged head can leave him breathless, the image of the young woman’s bleeding forehead flashing behind his eyes. Sometimes, a dull ache in his ribs on a damp morning is enough to transport him back to the pavement, the scent of asphalt and fear filling his senses. He finds himself constantly checking over his shoulder when he walks to his car after work, certain that he is being followed, that the threat he faced that day is still out there, looking specifically for him. He has spent countless nights replaying the event, trying to understand what he did wrong. There is something about me that made the event happen, he thinks. If he hadn't stood so close to the front, if his voice hadn't been so loud in the chants, perhaps he wouldn't have been singled out. The shame of this belief is a constant, heavy companion.

This internal conviction that he is somehow flawed has carved out a chasm between him and everyone else. His ex-wife, who left three months ago, said she felt like she was living with a ghost. He couldn't explain the fear, the need to check the locks three times before bed, or why he could no longer stand to be in a crowd. He felt fundamentally different from other people, as if he were marked by an experience they could never comprehend. He feels isolated and set apart from others, watching the world continue on from behind a pane of glass. The isolation, combined with the persistent fear and self-blame, has hollowed him out. Lately, a new and terrifying thought has taken root: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore. It was the frequency of this thought, its quiet insistence, that finally scared him enough to make a call. He looks at the therapist now, the hope for relief warring with the deep-seated fear that he is permanently broken.
